verdict: Lend selectively to income-producing Gurugram office assets with signed leases and conservative LTV; decline pure pre-leasing construction exposure until the data pack score is available.
title: Gurugram Commercial Real Estate: a note to the credit manager
narrative:
## What the business physically is
Commercial real estate here means Grade A office floors built on Golf Course Road and similar corridors, then leased or sold to corporates. **Cash comes from rent or sale proceeds, not from the building itself.** Lodha's new Golf Course Road project is 4 lakh sq ft of saleable area on 1.2 acres, with investment of Rs 1,100-1,200 crore [1][3]. So when a proposal lands, check whether the borrower is selling floors or holding them for rent; the two have completely different repayment logic.

## Where value and cash sit
**Value sits in the lease or sale contract, and cash sits in the tenant's payment cycle.** Peers show the pattern: Brigade's average realisation rose 29% year-on-year to Rs 13,841 per square foot [5], while Phoenix Mills' office income rose 64% on higher occupancy [7]. Brigade's Q3 net profit fell 21% to Rs 186.5 crore even as revenue rose, because margin contracted [4]. So ask for the rent roll and the tenant mix; if occupancy is rising but margin is slipping, ask why.

## What has changed now
**A large Mumbai developer has just entered Gurugram with a Rs 1,200 crore office project [1][2][3], which tells you capital is chasing this corridor.** That is good for exit values and bad for weaker landlords who will face newer, better buildings. The data pack gives no score for this industry or state [D], so I cannot give you a numeric cut-off. **Treat the missing score as a reason to underwrite the asset, not the market story.**

## Who to pursue and how to grow safely
**Pursue owners of operational, leased office assets with named tenants and a track record of collections; avoid pure land aggregators and first-time developers pre-leasing.** Structure against rent receivables, keep LTV conservative, and take a covenant on occupancy and on tenant concentration. Every month take the rent roll, the bank statement of the rental account, and the list of tenants with dues. If a single tenant is above a third of income, ask for a lease-copy review before disbursal.

## Early-warning signs
**Watch for rent discounts, rising vacancy, and refinancing of construction loans into rental-backed debt.** Rating material flags refinancing risk where debt is in commercial paper and NCDs with bullet maturities [9][11], and notes that operational assets typically refinance construction loans against expected rentals [10]. If a borrower asks to refinance a construction loan before occupancy stabilises, ask for the signed leases first. If monthly rent collections fall below the prior quarter, stop fresh disbursal and review the account.
watch: Collections fall below prior quarter -> freeze fresh disbursal and review tenant dues
Single tenant above one-third of income -> seek lease copies and reprice risk
Pre-leasing below plan at refinance request -> decline refinance until leases are signed
Coverage falls below the level at sanction -> seek promoter support or additional security
